prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A last rock-skip hurlstorm (crazing river-glass) the closest they ever were. • In right lockstitch snared and split some fire-supper cooked on sticks. • By dawn the older brother took to chucking what bottle-frags he could find and crud-oysters across. The (high-pitched) younger blacked our waters with a yowl. • Lord the sound such as rose from him carried so— Carved into us. Clings. • Hadn’t they clung tooth and claw to branch and bark. — Came a man (and truck) to take them off. • Dieseled those boys off away some say somewheres upcountry, inland. • Where it was they landed (why) nobody not them knows. • No body not them knows just how they humped and grubbled home what road they’d graved what woods criss-crossed which creeks which trains they’d hopped who helped. • Came safe home sure but blank as houses. Came safe home —as him —and him. —as (evermore) not them.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Lord, Carved

outputs.L1: A last rock-skip hurlstorm—crazing the river-glass—the closest they ever were. • Snared in right lockstitch, they split a fire-supper cooked on sticks. • By dawn, the older brother had taken to chucking across whatever bottle-frags and crud-oysters he could find. The high-pitched younger blacked our waters with a yowl. • Lord, the sound that rose from him carried so—carved itself into us. Clings. • Hadn’t they clung, tooth and claw, to branch and bark. —Then came a man—and a truck—to take them off. • Dieseled those boys away, some say, somewhere upcountry, inland. • Where they landed—and why—nobody, not even they, knows. • Nobody, not even they, knows how they humped and grubbled home; what road they’d graved, what woods criss-crossed, which creeks, which trains they’d hopped, who helped. • Came safe home, sure, but blank as houses. Came safe home—as him—and him. —As, evermore, not them.
outputs.L2:
The nearest they ever came to one another was during a final barrage of skipping stones that shattered the river’s glassy surface. Working together in perfect rhythm, they caught and divided a meal roasted over the fire on sticks. By morning, the elder brother was throwing whatever shards of bottles and foul oysters he could gather across the water. The younger one, his voice shrill, stained our waters with his howl. Lord, how far that cry traveled. It cut itself into us and remains there still.

Hadn’t those boys held on with teeth and nails to every limb and strip of bark? Then a man arrived in a truck and pulled them down. People say he drove them away in that diesel vehicle, somewhere inland, somewhere upriver. Where they were left—or why—no one knows, not even the boys themselves. No one but they can know how they struggled and scavenged their way back: what roads they traced, what forests they crossed and recrossed, which streams they forded, which trains they caught, or who gave them aid.

They returned alive, certainly, but emptied out like abandoned houses. They came home safely as this one and that one—yet forever no longer themselves.
outputs.L3:
The brothers endured a violent and desperate ordeal by the river, surviving only by clinging to branches, strips of bark, and whatever else they could grasp. Through the darkness, they fought the current and their own exhaustion, holding on until dawn.

When morning finally came, the older brother began throwing bottle fragments and pieces of debris across the water, perhaps hoping to attract attention. Beside him, the younger brother cried out with a piercing desperation. Eventually, a man arrived in a truck. He took the boys far inland, carrying them to a place they did not know.

What happened afterward remains unclear. No one knows exactly how the brothers found their way home, which roads they followed, or what woods and creeks they crossed. It is equally uncertain whether they traveled by train or received help from strangers along the way. Their return can be traced only through fragments and unanswered questions.

In the end, both boys made it home safely. Yet survival did not mean that they returned unchanged. The ordeal had hollowed something out inside them, leaving them emotionally empty and fundamentally altered by what they had endured.
outputs.L4:
The narrative unfolds through fractured scenes, dense local dialect, and dreamlike images of river, mud, darkness, and movement. At its center are two brothers whose lives are rooted in a river home that provides not only shelter but also identity, memory, and belonging. Their world is shattered when they are seized and violently carried away. The removal is described less as a clear sequence of events than as a rush of confused sensations—harsh voices, unfamiliar hands, fear, and the sudden loss of the landscape that has always made them feel secure.

Separated from everything familiar, the brothers struggle to find their way back. Their return takes on a mysterious, almost mythic quality, as though they are moving through both real terrain and the disordered space of trauma. The fragmented language reflects their confusion and helplessness: events seem to break apart, time becomes uncertain, and the boundary between memory, nightmare, and reality grows indistinct. Throughout the ordeal, the brothers remain bound to each other, yet even that bond cannot fully protect them from what has been done to them.

Eventually, they reach their river home again. On the surface, the ending appears fortunate: both brothers have survived, and neither shows an obvious physical wound. Yet their safety is only partial. They return silent, distant, and emotionally hollowed out, unable to recover the sense of wholeness they possessed before their removal. Home remains physically present, but it can no longer offer the same comfort, because the experience of displacement has permanently altered their relationship to it.

The text therefore refuses the idea that returning home automatically repairs loss. The brothers’ bodies come back, but some essential part of them does not. Through its broken structure, dialect-rich voice, and haunting imagery, the narrative reveals trauma as an enduring internal wound. Displacement is shown not merely as separation from a place, but as a violent disruption of identity, memory, and belonging—one that continues even after the journey home is complete.
outputs.L5:
### The Lord Carved

The Lord carved rivers through the mountains  
and filled their silver veins with rain.  
He carved valleys beneath the clouds,  
where wildflowers woke from winter’s sleep.

Yet His finest work was not stone or sky,  
nor the moon suspended over the sea.  
With patience, sorrow, joy, and love,  
the Lord carved hope into the human heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental Southern Gothic prose poem about two brothers stranded across a river, taken away by truck, and eventually returning home profoundly changed. Use fragmented syntax, dialect, parentheticals, and haunting repetition.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the River Kept**

Across the river stood the brothers, though stood ain’t the word for it. More like waited. More like had been set down by some large hand and forgot. Cottonwoods worrying their black leaves. Water fat with moon. No bridge—not since the flood took it, pilings and hymnbooks and all.

Eli called, *We over here.*

Jonah called, *Ain’t we.*

Their mother heard them from the porch (or dreamed she did), two voices sewn into one wet voice: *Mama, Mama, the river won’t let us cross.*

Then the truck came.

No lamps. No plates. A pale cab shivering at the bank, engine coughing up flies. The driver wore Sunday gloves and had no Sunday face. Get in, he said. Or maybe the river said it. Or maybe no one said nothing and the brothers climbed inside because boys will enter any darkness that opens a door.

The truck took them south. Took them under the cypress knees, past the slaughterhouse, past fields where scarecrows bowed without wind. Took them where the road narrowed to a scar.

Gone, gone.

Their mother left two plates cooling. Left them till the gravy skinned over, till June rotted into August, till folks quit asking and commenced remembering wrong. One drowned, they said. Both drowned. Never were two. (There had always been two.) At night she heard the truck in the walls, gears grinding behind the plaster.

Years later—though the calendar swore it was only Thursday—the brothers came walking up the red road.

Eli taller. Jonah thin as a gate hinge. Their hair gone white at the temples, their hands smelling of diesel and river mud. Neither cast a shadow. Or both cast the same one.

Mama, said Eli.

Ma’am, said Jonah.

She opened the screen, but they did not cross. Could not, seemed like. Just stood in the yard with the rain passing through their coats.

What’d they do to y’all? she asked.

The brothers looked toward the river.

It was moving backward.

Nothing, they said.

Nothing, nothing.

And from far off—or beneath the house—came the low truck rumble, coming closer, coming home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, modernist paragraph in the style of Faulkner-inflected Appalachian folklore. Include boys throwing bottle shards and oyster shells, a younger brother’s terrible cry, a mysterious man with a diesel truck, and the brothers’ unexplained journey home.
counterfactuals.output: By dusk the boys had climbed above the abandoned tipple where the laurel grew black and close as old women whispering, and from that high shelf of shale they flung green bottle shards and oyster shells—though no ocean lay within three hundred miles—down onto the rusted roofs below, watching each pale shell wheel like a broken moon, until the younger brother gave forth that terrible cry, not pain exactly but recognition, as if something beneath the mountain had called him by the name he had before he was born; and then the man appeared beside the haul road, hatless, gray-eyed, his diesel truck idling with the patient thunder of buried machinery, and though neither boy afterward could remember his words, or whether he spoke at all, they climbed in, carrying the smell of glass dust and creek mud with them, and rode through hollows they did not know, past houses lit from within by blue fire, past a church whose bell swung soundlessly, until they found themselves walking at dawn along their own fence line, barefoot and empty-handed, while behind them the mountain kept its smoke and the road showed no tracks, and their mother, standing in the doorway as if she had been standing there forever, asked no question, only touched the younger boy’s throat where the cry had gone and would not come again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn the story of two feral-seeming brothers separated from home and transported upcountry into lyrical, disjointed prose. Emphasize sound, communal memory, uncertainty, and the idea that although they returned safely, they were no longer themselves.
counterfactuals.output:
They came out of the scrub on all fours—or so the village remembers.

Memory has many mouths.

Some say the brothers bit when touched. Some say they only trembled. Their hair was full of burrs, their knees lacquered with mud, and in their throats lived a small animal sound: not crying, not speech, but something between a cough and a bird striking glass.

Then the engine.

Iron clatter. Whistle-scream. Wheels beating the earth into a single word:

gone, gone, gone.

Upcountry, where the hills rose dark as sleeping cattle, strangers lifted them down. The boys did not give their names. Or gave the wrong names. Or had forgotten that names were things one could carry.

At home, the village repeated them anyway.

At dusk the women called into the trees. The old men argued over footprints. Children invented sightings: two pale faces beside the river, two shadows stealing milk, two wolves wearing the torn shirts of boys.

Weeks passed. Perhaps months. Time frayed.

And then—returned.

A cart at noon. Dust opening. Their mother running until her breath broke.

Yes, they were alive. Yes, every finger. Every tooth. No grave to dig, no mourning cloth to unfold. The village made noise enough to frighten death away: bells, bowls, laughter, hands striking shoulders, voices piling upon voices.

But the brothers stood inside the celebration like strangers in rain.

They listened for the engine beneath every silence.

They slept with their shoes on. They turned when no one called. One spoke too softly; the other not at all. In mirrors, they searched behind their own faces.

Safe, everyone said.

Home, everyone said.

Yet something had remained upcountry—or something had followed them back.

Years later, no one could agree on what the boys had been before. Gentle, said one. Wild, said another. Always quiet. Always singing.

Memory has many mouths, and none of them speak the whole truth.

Only this: two brothers vanished.

Two brothers returned.

And between those sentences, the rails kept singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem narrated by a river or collective landscape remembering two lost boys. Use bullet-like separators, abrupt clauses, invented words such as “hurlstorm” or “grubbled,” and recurring phrases like “nobody knows” and “came safe home.”
counterfactuals.output:
• I carried their names under my tongue of stones. Two boys, red-capped, rain-kneed, running where the alder roots went grubbled into dusk. They said they would cross me. They said they knew the way. Nobody knows.

• Above us, the hurlstorm unstitched the hills. Heather flew. Fences bowed their black backs. The boys became two brief lanterns in the weather—then one—then none.

• We were all listening: river, bracken, bog, the sheep-track filling with rain. Abrupt dark. A shout snapped short. Nobody knows whether it was a name or only a crow turned inside out by wind.

• All night I searched myself. Every pool. Every silvered undercut. I asked the reeds; they hissed. I asked the bridge; it kept its one cold eye. The mountain said nothing, having swallowed its mouth.

• Down in the village, windows burned like small held breaths. Mothers counted footsteps. Fathers carried ropes, lamps, the old impossible hope. One searcher came safe home. Then another came safe home. The dogs came safe home, mud-starred and shivering.

• But not the boys.

• Spring entered slowly, greenfingering the banks. Summer laid gold on the ford. Still I remembered: two shadows leaning over my bright skin, laughing at minnows, daring the deep. Nobody knows where laughter goes when the mouth is gone.

• Years huddled and passed. Their names grew moss-soft on the stone. Children who had never seen them threw twigs into me and watched them race. I bore each twig gently. I tried to make every small thing come safe home.

• Listen: in flood-time I still call them. In drought I show my ribs. The hills bend closer. The bog bubbles its black syllables. We are one remembering body, root and rain, feather and fell.

• Two boys. Abrupt light. Hurlstorm. Grubbled dark.

• Nobody knows.

• Nobody knows.

• Yet each night I carry them to the sea, and each dawn the sea returns them as mist, and the mist climbs the mountain, and for one pale hour they come safe home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a highly stylized literary passage about brothers clinging to branches, cooking food over a fire, hurling debris across dark water, being removed by a man in a truck, and finding their way back by unknown roads, woods, creeks, and trains. End on an eerie note of irreversible alienation.
counterfactuals.output:
The brothers lived for a while in the green fists of the sycamores, clinging where the branches forked above the river. Below them, the water moved blackly, carrying stars in broken pieces. They slept with bark printed into their cheeks and woke feathered with leaves, as if the trees had been trying all night to claim them.

At dusk they climbed down and built a fire from twigs, rags, and the splintered slats of an abandoned chair. In a dented pan they cooked whatever the day had given them: two small fish, an onion gone soft, beans from a can opened with a stone. Smoke folded around their faces. Grease hissed like rain. They ate with their fingers and licked the salt from their wrists.

Afterward, for no reason they could name, they hurled things across the dark water—bottles, bricks, rusted gears, handfuls of gravel. Each object vanished before it struck. Then, after a pause, came the distant sound: a gulp, a bell, a mouth closing. They threw harder, as though the far bank had insulted them, as though somewhere beyond sight stood another pair of brothers throwing the whole ruined world back.

The man arrived before dawn in a truck the color of old bone. He wore gloves though it was summer. He did not ask their names. He pinched out their fire beneath his boot, took them one by one from the branches, and put them in the truck among coils of rope, empty fuel cans, and a shovel polished bright at the blade.

They rode for hours beneath a canvas cover. Whenever they lifted its edge, the road had changed.

First there were warehouses leaning over weeds. Then fields furred with mist. Then woods in which the trees stood too close together, their trunks pale and listening. The man left them near a town whose church had no clock, pointing with one gloved hand toward houses shuttered against the morning.

But the brothers turned back.

They found no road they knew. Still, they walked. They followed deer paths, drainage ditches, the silver seams of creeks. They crossed beneath bridges where trains thundered overhead, shaking black dust into their hair. Once they climbed into an open freight car and slept among sacks of seed, waking three counties away—or thirty years; neither could tell. They learned to trust the direction in which dogs barked, the tilt of moss, the low blue rumor of water beyond a hill.

Sometimes they found their footprints already waiting in the mud.

Sometimes, deep in the woods, they heard stones striking water.

At last the river appeared between the trees, narrow and dark as a slit in the earth. The sycamores still leaned above it. Their branches held the pale scars of the brothers’ hands. Their fire ring remained on the bank, filled now with rainwater and drowned moths.

They climbed eagerly, each to his old fork.

But from across the river came two voices, whispering from the darkness in tones exactly their own. The voices spoke of roads the brothers had never taken, meals they had never eaten, years they did not remember living. Then the unseen things on the opposite bank began hurling debris—bottles, bricks, rusted gears—which vanished midway and landed softly at the brothers’ feet.

Only then did they understand: they had found their way back, but not to the side of the water where they had begun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
